source_caption:
Thirteen is such an uncomfortable movie, but that’s also what makes it so good.

Tracy is 13 when she becomes fascinated by Evie and the life she seems to have figured out. She starts changing herself to fit into this new world, and before long, she’s becoming someone completely different.

What I really like about the movie is that it never feels like Tracy just wakes up one day and becomes a different person. It happens slowly. One choice leads to another, and she keeps going further without really knowing where it’s all heading.

Her relationship with her mother makes it even more painful to watch. There’s clearly a lot of love between them, but they just don’t know how to reach each other anymore.

Evan Rachel Wood is amazing here, and Holly Hunter is equally great. The whole movie feels incredibly raw and honest, especially for something made over 20 years ago.

🎥: Thirteen (2003)
Dir. Catherine Hardwicke

source_details.synopsis: Thirteen is a 2003 psychological coming-of-age teen drama film directed by Catherine Hardwicke, written by Hardwicke and Nikki Reed and starring Holly Hunter, Evan Rachel Wood and Reed with Jeremy Sisto, Brady Corbet, Deborah Kara Unger, Kip Pardue, Sarah Clarke, D. W. Moffett, Vanessa Hudgens (in her film acting debut), and Jenicka Carey in supporting roles. Loosely based on Nikki Reed's life at ages 13 to 14, the film's plot follows Tracy, a middle school student in Los Angeles, who begins dabbling in substance abuse, sex, and crime after becoming friends with the school's popular girl, Evie. The screenplay for Thirteen was written over six days by Hardwicke and the then-14-year-old Reed;
